item.title: The Words We Use Can Change How We See Dementia
item.description:
Dementia

The Words We Use Can Change How We See Dementia

The language of dementia can shape whether we see a diagnosis or a whole human.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Labels can turn a behavior someone is experiencing into an identity we assign to them.
  • Language can reinforce dementia stigma or help us see the whole person living with brain change.
  • The words we choose can either narrow the lens through which we see someone with dementia or widen it.

Imagine a man who gets up repeatedly and walks toward the door of his memory care community. We could call him a wanderer, which is a word that has been used for decades in dementia care. Or we could ask where he is trying to go. Imagine a woman who becomes distressed every afternoon and repeatedly calls out for her husband. We could call her a yeller, or we could wonder what happens for her when the light begins to change, the room gets busier, or she realizes she cannot find the person who has made her feel safe for fifty years. Those may sound like small differences in language, but I don't think they are. The words we choose do more than describe what we see. They can influence what we look for next.

Words Become Lenses

Source: MMD Creative/Shutterstock

As a caregiver-turned-board-certified neuropsychologist, I have spent much of my life listening to the language we use around dementia. Dementia sufferer. Wandering. Difficult. Burden. She's not the same person anymore. Most people who use these words are not trying to be unkind. Many of these terms grew out of medicine and caregiving, and some remain common in clinical and research settings. But language doesn't simply communicate information. It also gives us a frame through which to interpret another human being. Language can either narrow the lens through which we see someone with dementia or widen it.

Source: Viktoria Kurpas/Shutterstock

A Wanderer or a Person Going Somewhere?

Consider again the man walking toward the exit at 4:30 every afternoon. If we decide that he is a wanderer, dementia itself can become the beginning and end of our explanation. He wanders because he has dementia. But what if he spent 40 years leaving work at 4:30? What if he believes his children are waiting for him? What if the room has become unbearably noisy and walking is his way of getting away from it? He may need the bathroom, be looking for someone familiar, feel restless after sitting most of the day, or simply want to go outside.

Changing our vocabulary doesn't magically give us the answer but what it can do is preserve a question. Contemporary person-centered approaches to dementia care encourage us to look beyond the neurological disease itself and consider a person's history, physical needs, emotional state, relationships, and environment when trying to understand behavior. Instead of assuming we already understand what the person is doing, we become curious about why it might make sense to them.

Different and the Same

Source: ArtemisDiana/Shutterstock

There is another sentence I have heard countless times from families: “She's not the same person anymore.” I understand what they mean, and I never want to use person-centered language to minimize what dementia can take from a person or a family. Dementia can profoundly change memory, language, judgment, personality, independence, and relationships. There is real loss in dementia, and the people who love someone with brain change may find themselves adapting to those losses again and again. But not the same person makes a much larger claim. It takes changes in some human capacities and turns them into a conclusion about the whole human being. I have come to prefer a sentence that makes room for both realities: She is different and the same.

article continues after advertisement

Dementia educator and occupational therapist Teepa Snow has helped bring this thinking into the language of everyday dementia care. Through her "Positive Approach to Care," she uses the language of brain change to focus attention on what is happening in a person's brain rather than allowing a diagnostic label to define the person. I have come to appreciate this language as brain change puts dementia back onto the spectrum of human experience.

After all, every one of us lives with a changing brain. Our brains change while we sleep and learn. They work differently when we are frightened, grieving, depressed, sleep-deprived, or hypoglycemic. None of these experiences is equivalent to the progressive neurodegeneration, but they remind us of something important: there is no group of people with perfectly stable, unchanging brains standing on one side of a line and a separate group of people with “changed brains” standing on the other.

Even Our Caring Words Matter

We can apply the same scrutiny to the language surrounding the people providing care. Consider the familiar phrase caregiver burden. There is no question that care partners can experience tremendous strain, and changing our vocabulary should never become a way of sanitizing that reality. But the word burden can blur an important distinction between the person and the demands of the situation. A husband may be exhausted without experiencing his wife as a burden.

This is one reason I have adopted the term care partner. For me, it is a small linguistic reminder that even when the balance of a relationship changes dramatically, there are still two human beings inside it. The point is not to become the language police. It is to become more conscious of what our language invites us to see and what it may allow us to stop seeing.

Source: KDS Productions

What Changing Brains Can Teach Us

Of course, none of this is only about dementia. Human beings categorize one another constantly. We talk about the difficult employee, the anxious child, the alcoholic, the homeless, the disabled, the elderly. There is a reason our brains do this. Categories are efficient and help an extraordinarily complicated brain organize an impossibly complicated social world. But efficiency comes with a risk: once we believe we know what someone is, we may become less curious about who they are.

article continues after advertisement

Dementia makes the consequences of that shortcut especially visible because cognitive abilities are so central to the way our culture measures independence, competence, and identity. As memory, language, reasoning, or independence change, it becomes remarkably easy for a complex human life to shrink in our language until the diagnosis is the only thing we see.

That is why changing our language about dementia is not about finding nicer words for a difficult disease. It is about trying to see more accurately. Better dementia language should be able to hold both realities at once: dementia can cause profound and painful change, and the person living with those changes remains more than the disease affecting their brain.

item.title: NYC: Keeping AI Out of Schools Doesn't Prepare Kids for It
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

NYC: Keeping AI Out of Schools Doesn't Prepare Kids for It

New York City just took one of the boldest steps in the U.S. on AI and children.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Keeping AI out of classrooms does not necessarily protect children from the AI they encounter elsewhere.
  • Just 90 minutes of AI instruction leaves out critical lessons on judgment, safety, privacy, and relationships.
  • Children need to learn how to question AI, verify its answers, protect privacy, and know when not to use it.

On Sept. 2, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for every child from 2-K through eighth grade. That’s nearly 600,000 students, roughly two-thirds of the district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, including high school. The city is also placing new limits on screen time, with recommended caps of 30 minutes per day for students in grades 3-5 and 45 minutes for students in grades 6-8.

Developmentally, this makes sense. Children need foundational skills before they can use a powerful tool like AI safely and wisely. They need opportunities to wrestle with a question, sit with not knowing, make mistakes, work through frustration, and build an argument before a machine builds it for them.

Those capacities are developed through effort and struggle. When a tool consistently removes that while these skills are still forming, it's a hindrance.

But the announcement leaves two big questions unanswered:

  • What happens when students go home?
  • How are we preparing them for a world in which AI will be everywhere?

Removing AI From School Does Not Remove It From a Child’s Life

According to Common Sense Media’s 2026 census of 1,204 American children ages 9 to 17, 86% already use or interact with AI, and 24% do so every day. Among 9- to 12-year-olds—the very students New York’s moratorium is designed to protect—81% use AI, and 17% use it daily.

Most are not encountering AI at school, either. More than three-quarters use AI on their own phone, computer, or tablet. Only 44% report using it on a school device.

Even if schools decide that students are not ready to use generative AI, that does not mean they are too young to learn about it. It simply means we recognize that AI is an inevitable and ubiquitous part of the world kids live in.

Parents can’t be expected to fill this gap. According to the Common Sense survey, 44% of children say a parent or guardian has never talked with them about how to use AI safely. Even among daily AI users, more than a third have never had that conversation.

So a student can leave an AI-free classroom and walk into a world full of AI—with no teacher nearby and, in many cases, no parent who has ever talked about it. And generative AI is only part of the picture. Artificial intelligence is already embedded in many of the technologies children use every day: YouTube and streaming recommendations, autocorrect and predictive text, navigation apps, search engines, filters, and learning platforms.

article continues after advertisement

Long before children open a chatbot, algorithms are already deciding what they see, what gets recommended to them, and what information rises to the top. We cannot ignore this reality.

AI Literacy Takes More Than 90 Minutes... in High School

For high school students—the students not covered by the moratorium—New York plans to provide two 45-minute AI literacy modules each year. Two. It actually pains me to type this.

The city says those 90 minutes will address what AI is and is not, bias, risks, ethical considerations, and the impact of AI on careers and future skills. These are all important topics, but each requires more than a single lesson. All require foundational knowledge built over time in order for the lesson to stick.

Consider what the city's short list leaves out:

  • How to verify AI output. Only about half of children surveyed by Common Sense Media say a school or teacher has ever talked with them about how to determine whether information generated by AI is accurate or trustworthy. Verification is not a fact students memorize. It is a habit they develop through repeated practice.
  • Why AI often agrees with them. AI systems are designed to be responsive and helpful. Students need to understand that a confident, agreeable answer is not necessarily a credible one.
  • Who owns what AI creates. Copyright, intellectual property, attribution, and creative ownership have become more complicated in the age of generative AI. Students need traditional media literacy to understand why these things matter.
  • What real human connection requires. New York is right to prohibit companion chatbots for students. But banning a category of technology does not teach children why a machine can simulate empathy without actually caring about them—or what healthy human relationships look like.
  • When not to use AI. This may be one of the most important skills of all. Students should learn to ask: Will this tool help me think, or will it do my thinking for me? Knowing when to refrain from using technology is a learned skill, too.
  • How algorithms already shape their lives. AI is increasingly involved in decisions about hiring, admissions, loans, benefits, policing, health, and more. To understand these systems later, students first need to understand concepts such as personal data, biometrics, profiling, recommendation systems, and algorithmic sorting. This is civic literacy.
  • What AI costs. AI has a significant environmental footprint, including energy use, water consumption, and the rapidly growing infrastructure required to support data centers. Many young people care deeply about environmental issues. They deserve to understand this part of the technology too.
  • What to do when something goes wrong. Of children who use chatbots, 17% say one has shown them something they felt was inappropriate or not meant for someone their age, and more than half told no adult. Knowing when and how to seek help is something children need to practice before they are in a difficult situation.
  • How to recognize synthetic media. Deepfakes, voice cloning, nudify apps, AI-enabled sextortion: these are things students are already encountering. They need the skills to recognize manipulation, understand consent, and know what to do when synthetic media is used to harm someone.
  • What they give away when they type in a prompt. Children need to understand that a conversation with an AI system is a conversation with a company collecting personal information about their bodies, health, family, relationships, and emotions.

And this is only a partial list; 90 minutes a year cannot do this work.

AI Literacy Is Not the Same as AI Use

New York’s moratorium gives educators an opportunity to protect childhood, preserve human-centered learning, and resist the rush to put powerful technology into students’ hands simply because it exists. But keeping AI out of elementary and middle school classrooms cannot mean keeping AI education out too. In fact, this may be exactly the moment to teach it.

article continues after advertisement

Students can learn how algorithms work without using a chatbot. They can investigate misinformation without generating it. They can practice protecting personal information without entering it into an AI tool. They can discuss bias, privacy, intellectual property, healthy relationships, environmental impact, and digital ethics without spending a minute looking at a screen. The strongest preparation may be decidedly low-tech: conversation, discussion, role-play, critical thinking, collaboration, media analysis, and opportunities to work through difficult questions with other human beings.

New York’s 600,000 children will spend this school year living in a world shaped by AI. Many will use it on their own devices, in their own bedrooms, without a teacher nearby and, for nearly half of them, without a parent who has ever talked with them about how to use it safely.

The question is not simply whether children should use AI in school. It is whether we are preparing them with the knowledge, judgment, and human skills they will need to live with it everywhere else.

item.title: What 'The Odyssey' Got Right From a Psychological Perspective
item.description:
Authenticity

What 'The Odyssey' Got Right From a Psychological Perspective

'The Odyssey' reflects the trauma recovery journey, your own hero's journey.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • 'The Odyssey' perfectly exemplifies the trauma recovery journey.
  • A hero's external challenges often mirror their internal landscape.
  • Surrendering ego and control is pivotal; true growth requires embracing vulnerability and loss.

Growing up in rural Ireland, life followed a quiet, predictable rhythm until classroom lessons on mythology, folklore, and literary classics completely blew my world open. From an early age, I was spellbound by the concept of the hero's journey—specifically, the “character development” that occurs when a mythological hero transforms pain into purpose. Becoming a trauma therapist was not a deliberate choice; in truth, I always wanted to become a writer. As a therapist, I could at least listen to people’s stories and partner with them to coauthor their future. Today, the therapy room feels like a modern arena for those same timeless myths. It has shown me that the ultimate character development doesn't just happen in ancient scrolls—it lives within all of us. Christopher Nolan’s new adaptation of The Odyssey perfectly exemplifies the trauma recovery journey. It is the quintessential tale of the hero: a person who leaves their ordinary world, faces trials and tribulations, and ultimately returns home wiser and stronger, transformed by the experience.

What 'The Odyssey' Got Right From a Psychological Perspective...

1. The Dark Night of the Soul as an Allegory for Personal Growth
Joseph Campbell explained that the hero's journey is not merely an external adventure of battling monsters. Instead, it is equally—if not more—about the psychological journey of confronting one’s fears, doubts, and insecurities: the shadow. Your “shadow” is the hidden, darker side of you—your repressed feelings, memories, weaknesses, destructive impulses, and unacknowledged desires. It is through the confrontation with your "shadow," which can take many forms—the most feared enemy, a painful memory, or an impossible task—that the seeker truly becomes a hero.

This predestined meeting with the inner "monster" (shadow) should be viewed as an opportunity rather than an obstacle; it is an initiation that forces you to turn inward, harness power, and overcome fear. A hero's external challenges often mirror their internal landscape. In The Odyssey, the mythical monsters and obstacles Odysseus encounters are psychological projections of his own internal conflicts, flaws, and desires. The lawless, myopic giant Cyclops, who refuses to honor the gods or the laws of hospitality (xenia), mirrors his toxic, ego-driven hubris, while the Sirens exploit his attachment to past glory and "broken promises." Trials like Calypso and Circe represent his deep-seated urge to abandon his heroic destiny for the comfort of indulging his animalistic impulses.

Ultimately, by defeating these external threats, Odysseus conquers his "shadow," the disowned parts of his identity. Conquering external foes ultimately leads to conquering the self, reminding us that when you defeat the enemy within, no enemy outside can do you harm. His journey to the Land of the Dead represents the ultimate confrontation with his psychological shadow. In Nolan's film adaptation, this is without a doubt the most powerful scene. As we are transported to this dark, subconscious realm, the monsters Odysseus faces are not beasts of flesh and bone, but the ghosts of his past. Meeting his fallen comrades from the Trojan War, one after another, forces him to reckon with the brutal reality of the violence, loss of human life, and
carnage he left behind in his pursuit of glory. Odysseus feels a chill creep through his bones; the weight of sacrifice is heavy in the air, and it all feels completely hollow now. To move forward, Odysseus must look past his warrior ego, accept his vulnerability, and swallow the bitter truths. This dark night of the soul is a period of intense suffering, a painful but necessary phase of destruction that sets the stage for profound rebirth and spiritual evolution.

article continues after advertisement

2. The Surrender: Weeping on Calypso’s Shores
The concept of surrender is often viewed as a defeat, but in the hero’s journey, it is a necessary ego-death. It is the complete loss of your sense of self. It forces you to unlearn everything that kept you small, to shed false identities, break lifelong conditioning, and embrace your vulnerability. You’ll experience a temporary or permanent loss of your identity, your perception will alter, your sense of personal control will melt away, and you will be forced to surrender. This is beautifully captured in the movie adaptation during Odysseus’s time on Calypso's island, weeping, numbing, and seeking comfort. Despite being offered physical immortality and a life of effortless luxury with a goddess, Odysseus surrenders his pride, his past glory, and the illusion of
control. He accepts his mortal limitations and acknowledges that a life hidden from his true purpose is no life at all. He enters the sea and lies on a piece of wooden debris, weak, vulnerable to the elements but hopeful. In the stillness and serenity of surrender, he is forced to find peace by aligning himself with the flow of life, trusting that he is capable and strong enough to handle whatever comes his way. This moment of absolute surrender to his mortal destiny is what allows the universe to divinely finally open the gates for his release, proving that one must let go of the life they planned to receive the life waiting for them.

3. The Homecoming
The final reunion in Ithaca is the crown jewel of the epic story arc; it models the process of "individuation," or returning to the self. Odysseus has developed grace and humility over the course of his 20 years of suffering. He does not walk through the front door seeking a garland; instead, he cautiously assesses, disguised as a lowly beggar in his own palace. He expects nothing and returns with an open and sincere heart. This is the ultimate sign of his internal growth; he has let go of his warrior pride while being insulted and struck by the suitors. When he finally reunites with his wife, Penelope, it is not just a physical return to a place, but a spiritual return to himself. He is no longer his ego but now a transformed, humble, and healed king. Like Odysseus, as you journey deeper into your healing journey, you will learn that you are slowly transforming into a more resilient and authentic version of yourself, finally coming home to the essence of who you are meant to be.

And What It Got Wrong…

While the film attempts to capture the grand scale of Greek mythology, it significantly flattens the psychological depth of its female characters. Ancient Greek lore is rich with complex, powerful female archetypes who embody a nuanced psychological blend of vices and virtues, light and darkness. Unfortunately, characters like Penelope, Athena, and Calypso feel severely underdeveloped in this cinematic adaptation. Instead of portraying their intricate internal motivations, this adaptation strips away their moral ambiguities and emotional conflicts, missing a vital psychological truth: that true strength lies in their complexity, not just their status.

item.title: Handling Dismissive Comments at Work
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Handling Dismissive Comments at Work

How women can respond to dismissive comments in the workplace.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Dismissive comments at work can undermine confidence.
  • Repeating dismissive remarks back to the speaker helps to expose their inappropriateness.
  • Don’t be shy about requesting support for poor behavior in the workplace.

Sometimes dismissive words at work can have a lasting impression and affect long-term career success.

When Marisa was 24 years old, just starting out in her career, she was asked by Phil, a senior executive at work, to go shopping for underwear for his girlfriend. She was taken aback by this request but decided to just go along with it.

On her lunch break, Marisa shopped for the underwear and presented it to him. A few days later, he requested that she shop again, but to make sure to purchase sexy underwear this time. She told Phil that she didn’t feel comfortable shopping again for his girlfriend.

She decided to discuss the situation with her boss as it made her feel uncomfortable around Phil. Her boss just dismissed the incident as silly. Dismissing an incident that makes someone feel uncomfortable as “silly” can lead to an unsafe workplace.

Marisa felt unsupported, and this incident stayed with her throughout her career. She eventually went on to start her own coaching and leadership company in Dubai focused on helping other women achieve success and support when they need it.

Dismissive comments at work undermine confidence, shut down idea creation, and can damage team morale. One way to handle these situations is to repeat back to the person exactly what they just said to you. For instance, Marisa could have said to Phil, “Did you just ask me to go buy sexy underwear for your girlfriend?”

To see how this approach can work, consider this scenario: Barbara, a senior marketing executive in a biotech company, was stating her views strongly in a meeting about the project she was presenting to the team and explaining why she was taking a different approach. John, a colleague, accused her of being mean. In this case, she did his comment back to him, and the entire room went silent. After waiting a few seconds, she continued her presentation.

Would a man ever accuse another man of being mean in a meeting? Not likely.

Often in the workplace, dismissive comments just get brushed aside. Barbara singled out a comment that made her feel and look weak, and simply by repeating it showed the group and the commenter that it was a stupid and damaging thing to say.

Women can take their power back by using this simple technique that gives them respect and enables the other person to see the inappropriateness of their request or comment.

item.title: The Hidden Pain of Adoptee Birthdays
item.description:
Adoption

The Hidden Pain of Adoptee Birthdays

For adoptees, birthdays can be reminders of grief and loss.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Adoptees may feel loss, identity confusion, and longing during joyful birthday celebrations.
  • The nervous system can hold implicit memories of early separation that resurface on birthdays.
  • Rituals like lighting a candle and placing a letter in a grief mailbox can help adoptees honor this day.

For most people, birthday celebrations are filled with cake, candles, and being told, “We’re so happy you were born.” For people, who were adopted, at birth or through foster care, some enjoy celebrating birthdays, others dread them, and for many adoptees, birthdays can feel like an unspeakable loss. As one adoptee said: “When they told me to make a wish before blowing out my candles, I always wished secretly to meet my birth mother.”

As a psychotherapist specializing in adoption and foster care, and as an adoptee myself, I understand that birthdays can carry a double meaning: a celebration of life and a reminder of loss. Both truths exist, and both are hard to carry at once. This day serves as a reminder of the separation from one's birth family, an agony of grief that is real, hidden, and not always recognized, validated, or openly acknowledged by society. Adoptees often keep this loss locked in an internal vault, leaving many holding a vessel of grief that has no clear place to go.

For adoptees, a birthday is not just the beginning of life. It is the day they were separated from their first connection…their birth mother. Even when there is no conscious memory, the body remembers this as separation trauma, as explored in the book The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk. Trauma research shows that early relational breaks are stored as implicit memory in the nervous system. So, while the outside world sings “Happy Birthday,” the inside world is feeling something entirely different, not because something is wrong, but because a profound loss has occurred.

So even if adoptees aren’t actively talking about this, that does not mean they are not actively thinking about this. Some common questions for adoptees on their birthdays are:

What was that day like for my first mother and for me?
Who celebrated my birth?
Was I held? Did she cry when I left?
Am I a memory or a mystery?

Do they think of me on my birthday?
Would they recognize me now?
What part of me comes from them?

How could any mother give away her baby?
Is there something wrong with me?
Was I not lovable?
Am I not worthy?

These questions live quietly beneath the surface, sometimes acted out as sadness, irritability, withdrawal, or even anger. The family of one child I worked with reported that during his birthday party, he just disappeared. His parents were confused about where he had gone and found him crying alone in his room. He couldn’t put into words what he was feeling in the moment, but when we explored this later in therapy, he said, “Everyone was so happy, and all I felt was alone, like I didn’t exist.” He was experiencing a grief reaction, also called a grief anniversary, the embodied feeling of separation and loss all over again.

article continues after advertisement

A New Way to Hold the Day: The Candle Ritual

One powerful intervention I use with adoptees, especially around birthdays, is a candle ritual. This ritual allows adoptees to honor both parts of their story: the life they are living and the connection they lost. This can be done the day before or on their birthday.

Here’s how it works:

  1. The adoptee decorates a candle that represents their birth parent or first family.
  2. The candle is lit, supervised by their parents.
  3. They are invited to sit with its warmth, allowing a quiet moment of connection, wondering about their first family.
  4. They can write a letter, saying everything they never got to say, including love, anger, grief, questions, and longing.
  5. The letter can be read out loud, giving voice to what has been held inside or placed in an envelope, next to the candle.
  6. Finally, the letter can be placed in their grief mailbox, another intervention in my treatment book. It's a box that holds unsent letters and cards. I will often write an adopted child a sympathy card on their birthday reading: “I am so sorry for your loss, the loss of not being with your birth family.”

The candle ritual and grief mailbox create something many adoptees never received: permission to feel all of it. This empowers them to feel what interferes with their celebration, have a place to hold questions that don’t have answers, and create a space to honor a part of their story, often coined the "ghost kingdom." The goal is not to take the grief away. The goal is to sit beside it.

article continues after advertisement

For parents, I recommend processing feelings a few days before the birthday, with reflective statements such as:
“I wonder if this day brings up a lot for you.”
“You can feel happy and sad today.”
"I'm so sorry for your loss."
“We don’t have to pretend this day is only one thing.”
“If you’re thinking about your birth family today, that makes sense.”
“You don’t have to carry these feelings alone.”
“I can sit with you in whatever comes up.”
“There’s room for every part of your story here.”
“You can tell me anything you’re feeling; I can handle it.”
“This day belongs to you, and we can honor it in whatever way feels right.”

Healing for adoptees does not mean the birthday becomes easy. It means the day becomes integrated. I was born and I was separated. Celebration does not erase the loss, and the loss does not erase the adoptee's worth. This day merits adopting all of their parts, which is essential to developing a true sense of self.

So the next time you think of an adoptee on their birthday, pause and have a moment of compassion to celebrate not just the part that is celebrated, but the part that is remembered.

When the invisible loss is acknowledged, the veil of aloneness begins to lift, the walls protecting pain slowly come down, and the mask concealing questions of one’s identity falls away. And in this newfound space between candlelight and truth, existence is redefined.

I invite you to listen to a poignant song, a moving testimony of what adoptees experience: "Mama Here, Mama Gone," written and performed by folk singer and adoptee Mary Gauthier.

item.title: Is It Madness or Something Else?
item.description:
Psychiatry

Is It Madness or Something Else?

How historians wrestle with using the correct terms to describe mental illness.

Posted September 3, 2026

Key points
  • Historians often debate about what terms should be used to describe mental illness experienced in the past.
  • Some terms that were once used by physicians have become offensive and are no longer used.
  • The term "madness" has been reclaimed and is used by the Mad People's Movement, Mad Pride, and Mad Studies.

In a few weeks, I’ll be teaching one of my favorite classes. “Madness and Society: From Ancient Times to the Present” pretty much does what it says on the tin. We examine the long and controversial history of mental health and illness, starting with the Ancient Greeks and Romans, charting the rise and fall of the asylum and the emergence of modern explanations and treatments. Along the way, we discuss the relationship between mental health and different themes, including religion, gender, race, and class. Throughout the class, I try to show how history helps us to understand why we explain and treat mental illness in the way we do today, potentially empowering us to change our approach for the better.

But what about that word “madness”? Why do I use that term instead of "mental illness" or something else? Here’s where it can get complicated for a historian.

Historians don’t like using anachronistic terms to describe what happened in the past. For instance, I have written about the many terms used to describe what began to be called attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in the 1980s.

The first description of a disorder that sounded like ADHD emerged in 1957: hyperkinetic impulse disorder highlighted hyperactivity and impulsivity, but didn’t mention inattentiveness specifically. Children with similar symptoms were sometimes diagnosed with minimal brain damage, but since that indicated some kind of brain injury (and not all children presented that way), the term minimal brain dysfunction eventually replaced it. Another term, Strauss syndrome (named after Alfred Strauss), was also used to describe children with similar symptoms who had evidence of brain injury.

In contrast, the term hyperkinetic reaction of childhood, found in the second edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, suggested that such symptoms were some kind of a response to external factors. Psychoanalysts often described such children as “acting out.” Finally, in DSM-III in 1980, the term attention deficit disorder (with or without hyperactivity) appeared, showing that not all children diagnosed with the disorder needed to be hyperactive, but then in 1987 the revised version of DSM-III brought hyperactivity back in again.

Rather than assuming that people using these disparate terms in the past meant exactly what we mean when we use the term ADHD, isn’t it better to figure out what they really meant? When we do that, we begin to realize that the history of ADHD is a little more complicated and nuanced than we might have assumed.

So let’s return to that term “madness.” Why do I use that and not another term? Some terms used to describe mental illness are considered offensive today. “Lunacy” and the related noun “lunatic,” for instance, come from a Latin term meaning struck by the moon or moonstruck. The term has been used for nearly 2,000 years in the Latin language and back to around 1300 in English. We see the terms lunatic and lunacy being used formally in the 19th century, for instance in the names of asylums and the English Lunacy Act of 1845. But for many decades the term has been considered offensive, partly due to the connotation that the moon has something to do with mental illness and partly due to the term's corruption into the slang term “loony,” as well as other factors.

Another term commonly used to describe mental illness in the past was “insanity.” Use of this term (and the term “insane”) goes back to the late 16th century, and we still see it being used today in legal settings when a lawyer invokes the “insanity defense.” Unlike the terms lunacy and lunatic, the term insanity doesn’t have a noun equivalent, which may make it slightly less offensive. Nevertheless, it isn’t used anymore in medical settings, so I’ve never considered calling my class “Insanity and Society.”

What about mental illness? While I have been tempted to call my class “Mental Illness and Society,” there are a couple of problems with this term. First, the terms “mental health” and “mental illness” don’t go back all that far back. Both can be dated to approximately the 18th century and didn’t become dominant until the 20th century. Second, there is the focus on illness. Calling mental illness mental illness asserts that the characteristics or behaviors exhibited by an individual are automatically a sign of some underlying pathology, disease, or disorder. And some people diagnosed with mental illness contest this, arguing that they are not ill at all.

And this brings me to the term “madness.” Madness has been used to describe wild, deluded, or imprudent behavior since the late 14th century. Like lunacy and insanity, it was used to describe facilities that housed the mentally ill, specifically madhouses. But it’s a little more generic and vague. Mad can mean “crazy,” but it can also mean angry. One of the reasons I chose to use it for the title of my class, however, is that it is the term reclaimed by “mad” people to describe themselves. To them, “mad” doesn’t necessarily mean mentally ill, not least because “madness” isn’t a medical term applied by doctors, but a reclaimed term that people are able to apply to themselves, a term people can take a certain pride in. Since the early 1970s, the reclamation of the term has led to the Mad People’s Movement, Mad Pride, and, more recently, Mad Studies.

So, there are some historical reasons for why I use the term madness as opposed to other terms. But probably the most important reason is that if madness is a term chosen by the mad, it’s also good enough for me.
